analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers from forcing patients into mandatory arbitration or blocking class action lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any of the three House committees it was sent to and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurance contracts often include fine-print clauses that say any dispute must be resolved in private arbitration instead of court, and that bar patients from joining class action lawsuits. This bill would outlaw both clauses in group and individual health plans, letting patients sue insurers in court and band together in class actions. It also says a judge, not an arbitrator, decides whether the ban applies. The bill was referred to three House committees but never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private health insurance who have a dispute with their plan — a denied claim, a billing error, a coverage fight. They would keep their right to go to court and to join class action lawsuits instead of being forced into a private arbitration process chosen by the insurer, where outcomes are not public and appeals are limited.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits group health plans and group or individual health insurance coverage from including any clause requiring arbitration of claims under the plan [S3].
Prohibits plans from including any limitation on an enrollee's ability to join a class action lawsuit about the administration of the plan [S3].

Says whether the ban applies to a given agreement must be decided by a court, not an arbitrator, even if the contract purports to delegate that decision to an arbitrator — a provision aimed at keeping insurers from routing the question into arbitration [S3].

Applies the ban through three parallel amendments: the Public Health Service Act, the Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA), and the Internal Revenue Code, covering both insurance issuers and employer group plans [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer group plans, which would lose the ability to steer patient disputes into arbitration and would face more class action exposure over claims denials and plan administration. Insurers would likely argue that this raises litigation and administrative costs, which could feed back into premiums.

drawbacks.text: Insurers and plan administrators could see higher litigation costs from more court cases and class actions, which they could pass on to premiums — the cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge; the bill text itself does not provide for any cost offset [S3].

The bill is written narrowly: it covers arbitration clauses in health insurance contracts but does not address forced arbitration in the broader health system, such as clauses used by hospitals, nursing homes, or employers across other benefits [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real and targeted: patients keep access to public courts and class actions for plan disputes. The main cost is more litigation for insurers and employer plans, with some risk that it shows up in premiums. The bill does not address forced arbitration elsewhere in health care, so its reach is limited.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and a Health subcommittee on the day it was introduced, but no committee ever scheduled a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023 [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Katie Porter introduced the bill on June 16, 2021, with six Democratic cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor [S1][S3][S4][S5].
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no action was recorded after that — no hearings, no markups, no floor vote appear in its complete action history [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill still sitting in committee, so all legislative action ended with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plans are better off: they never had to give up mandatory arbitration clauses or face the added class action exposure the bill would have created. No patient gained anything because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Reps. Lloyd Doggett, Jan Schakowsky, Rosa DeLauro, and Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor vote was ever held, so there is no roll-call record of support or opposition; the bill's 7 cosponsors were all Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: Mandatory arbitration clauses let insurers resolve patient disputes privately, without juries or public records, and class action limits prevent patients from pooling small claims. The bill removes both tools. (No recorded opposition appears in the record; the bill simply died in committee.)
ERISA plans would lose the same arbitration and class action protections in disputes over plan administration, raising litigation exposure for employers and their plan administrators.
Private arbitrators and arbitration service firms lose a stream of health-plan disputes if the clause is banned; the public gains a court forum instead.
